Learning Objectives
Understand the anatomic landmarks for portal placement for knee arthroscopy.
Understand the components of a diagnostic knee arthroscopy.
Procedure
Indications

Indications
Knee arthroscopy continues to be the most commonly performed surgical procedure in
orthopaedics.1 Knee arthroscopy has a variety of uses that range from diagnostic to

therapeutic. Management of chondral, ligament, and meniscal pathologies are common
indications for knee arthroscopy. Management of the tearing of medial cartilage or
meniscus accounts for one-third of knee arthroscopy, followed by chondromalacia of the
patella, tearing of the lateral cartilage/meniscus, and management of cruciate ligament
injuries.2 Management of osteoarthritis, in part because of lack of evidence supporting
its effectiveness, accounts for only about 5% of procedures.2 Management of patellar
clunk, synovial biopsy, synovectomy, and septic arthritis are other uses of knee
arthroscopy.
Contraindications

Contraindications
No absolute contraindications exist for knee arthroscopy; however, patient factors, such
as morbid obesity and prior surgery, should be considered. A large body habitus may
make the successful completion of the goals of arthroscopy difficult. Prior surgery must
be considered before creating portals to avoid damage to nerves and vessels. Some
conditions, such as advanced osteoarthritis, are not appropriate for management via
arthroscopy.
Techniques
Preoperative Planning

Preoperative Planning
Review patient history, physical examination, and preoperative imaging studies to
determine the most likely pathologies to be addressed. Diagnostic arthroscopy at the
beginning of the procedure is essential to address all pathology.

Positioning

Positioning
Place the patient supine on the surgical table. The knee should be able to be moved
from full extension to flexion. A leg holder or post often is placed to allow valgus stress
of the knee and to better visualize the medial compartment. If a leg holder is used,
careful attention should be paid to ensure that the leg holder does not compress the
lateral femoral cutaneous nerve. The nonsurgical leg often is placed in a well-leg holder
or padded for safety.
Surgical Approaches
Getting Started
Surface anatomy: Palpate and mark or note the borders of the patella, patellar tendon, and
tibial tubercle. Also note the joint line, recalling that the lateral joint line is superior to the
medial joint line.
A vertical or horizontal incision is made through the skin and capsule. A vertical incision may
allow for more superior-inferior movement of instruments. A horizontal incision will allow
more medial-lateral mobility and will be in line with Langer lines. Consider the goal of surgical
management in selecting the orientation of the portals.
After the incision through the skin and capsule is made, the knife is pointed superiorly to
protect the meniscus. Then, the trocar is placed into the knee joint. The trocar can be
advanced medially and posterior to the Hoffa fat pad to clear space.
Extend the knee and advance the trocar into the suprapatellar space. Replace the trocar with
the camera.
If an outflow portal is desired, it can be made via a stab incision at this time. In determining
placement of the outflow portal (superolateral or superomedial), the surgical procedure being
performed must be considered.
Portals should be placed superiorly or inferiorly relative to the joint line accounting for patella
alta or baja.
Primary Portals
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:31 PM
AAOS | Knee Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002093
3/15

Anterolateral portal
This standard portal is most often used to begin diagnostic knee arthroscopy and serves as
the primary viewing portal.
To create this portal, flex the knee to 90°. The soft spot just lateral to the patellar tendon is the
primary landmark for this portal. If vertical incisions are made, the superior aspect of this
portal often can be located by creating the portal at the level of the inferior pole of the patella.
To ensure proper placement, a spinal needle can be used, directed toward the notch, to create
easy passage into the knee.• Anteromedial portal
Standard portal for primary instrumentation
With knee flexed to 90° and under direct visualization, place a spinal needle medial to the
patellar tendon, just above the joint line, in the soft spot.
When clearly above the medial meniscus, use an 11-blade scalpel with the blade pointed up
to make an incision through the skin and the capsule.
This portal should be adjusted based on the procedure being performed. For instance, this
portal should be lower, just above the anterior medial meniscus, for débridement or repair
of the posterior medial meniscus. Conversely, this portal should be higher for the
management lateral meniscus tears if instruments need to clear the tibial spine.
Superomedial portal
Accessory portal, often used for outflow
Make a stab incision superior and medial to the patella with the knee in extension.
May allow for evaluation of patellar tracking and medial facet cartilage injuries
Keeping this portal distal to the vastus medialis obliquus may limit postoperative pain at the
portal site.
Superolateral portal
Accessory portal, often used for outflow and useful for removing large loose bodies
Make a stab incision superior and lateral to the patella with the knee in extension.
May allow for evaluation of the lateral facet of the patella
Secondary Portals
Posteromedial portal
Use: visualization and instrumentation of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus, the
posteromedial joint space, and the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL)
Location: posterior to the medial collateral ligament, 1 cm proximal to joint line
Caution: saphenous nerve

Posterolateral portal
Use: visualization of the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus and the PCL
Location: between the lateral collateral ligament and the biceps tendon, 1 cm proximal to
joint line
Caution: peroneal nerve
Transpatellar portal
Use: central viewing portal
Location: central portion of the patellar tendon, 1 cm distal to the inferior pole
For bone-patellar tendon-bone reconstruction of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), this
portal may be placed through the tendon harvest site. The portal should not be established
through the patellar tendon before graft harvest.
Can be used as a working portal for articular cartilage surgery, such as osteochondral
allograft transplantation, because it allows for perpendicular access to some areas of the
femoral condyles.
Techniques
Diagnostic Scope
Diagnostic arthroscopy can be performed after establishing your viewing portal or after
creating your primary working portal so that structures can be addressed sequentially.
Regardless, diagnostic arthroscopy should be performed in the same manner in every patient
to ensure no structures are missed.
Suprapatellar pouch: Start by examining the suprapatellar pouch with the knee in full
extension. Turn the camera to look up to examine the cartilage of the medial and lateral
patellar facets (Figure 1).

Figure 1 Arthroscopic images show the medial (A) and lateral (B) facets of the patella. (Images
courtesy of Drew Landsdown, MD, San Francisco, CA, and Kendall Bradley, MD, Durham, NC.)
Patellofemoral joint: Turn your eyes medial to examine the patellofemoral joint, and gently flex
and extend the knee to observe patellar tracking. Note the condition of the trochlear groove at
this time. Cartilage of the patellofemoral joint and all compartments of the knee should be
evaluated based on the Outerbridge classification of cartilage (Figure 2; Table 1).3
Table 1 Outerbridge Classification of Cartilage
Grade
Description
I
Softening and swelling of cartilage
II
Fragmentation and fissuring <0.5 inches in diameter
III
Fragmentation and fissuring >0.5 inches in diameter
IV
Erosion of cartilage down to bone

Figure 2 Arthroscopic image shows the patellofemoral joint. (Image courtesy of Drew
Landsdown, MD, San Francisco, CA, and Kendall Bradley, MD, Durham, NC.)
Lateral gutter: Move your camera back into the pouch and turn your camera down as you
move laterally into the lateral gutter. You often will need to pull back slightly as you travel
down the gutter to avoid synovial folds, such as plica. The light cord can be gently rotated to
look back toward the joint as the level of the joint is approached to visualize the popliteus and
hiatus (Figure 3). This is an area where loose bodies often are observed. Visualize the fascicles
of the lateral meniscus adjacent to the popliteal hiatus. Pull back gently to observe the outer
rim and the anterior horn of the lateral meniscus. Then, drive the camera back into the
suprapatellar pouch and then medially to go down to the medial gutter. Take care to avoid
articular cartilage injury in the patellofemoral joint when transitioning between the gutters.

Figure 3 Arthroscopic image shows the popliteal fossa. (Image courtesy of Drew Landsdown,
MD, San Francisco, CA, and Kendall Bradley, MD, Durham, NC.)
Medial gutter: Travel down the medial compartment, with the camera again pointing back to
the joint. Loose bodies or peripheral medial meniscus tears may be observed (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Arthroscopic image shows the outer rim of the body of the medial meniscus. (Image
courtesy of Drew Landsdown, MD, San Francisco, CA, and Kendall Bradley, MD, Durham, NC.)

Medial compartment: Move into the medial compartment by gently flexing the knee and
applying a valgus stress on the knee (using the post or leg holder). Point the camera toward
the notch. Examine the medial meniscus and the cartilage of the medial femoral condyle and
the tibial plateau (Figure 5). An anteromedial portal may be established at this time. With a
calibrated probe, carefully probe the meniscus on its superior and inferior surfaces. Also
carefully interrogate the posterior root attachment. Further evaluation depends on
preoperative imaging studies and suspected pathology. For articular cartilage lesions, the knee
may be ranged through flexion and extension to visualize the entire condyle. To evaluate the
anterior horn and body of the meniscus, the camera may be rotated away from the notch.
Figure 5 Arthroscopic image shows the medial compartment and the posterior horn of the
medial meniscus. (Image courtesy of Drew Landsdown, MD, San Francisco, CA, and Kendall
Bradley, MD, Durham, NC.)
Intercondylar notch: evaluation of ACL/PCL (Figure 6)
Trace the notch to ensure the ligamentum/fat pad is not entered.
Probe the ACL for laxity.
Observe the PCL with its synovial lining.

Figure 6 Arthroscopic image shows the anterior cruciate ligament and the notch. (Image
courtesy of Drew Landsdown, MD, San Francisco, CA, and Kendall Bradley, MD, Durham, NC.)
Lateral compartment
Place a varus stress on the knee to open the lateral compartment (gentle varus or more
commonly figure-of-4 position).
As with the medial compartment, probe the lateral meniscus, cartilage of the lateral femoral
condyle and the tibial plateau, and meniscal root (Figure 7).

Figure 7 A and B, Arthroscopic images show the lateral compartment and the meniscal root.
(Images courtesy of Drew Landsdown, MD, San Francisco, CA, and Kendall Bradley, MD,
Durham, NC.)
Posteromedial compartment4
Use the Gillquist maneuver to view the posteromedial compartment.
At 90° of knee flexion, place the camera between the PCL and the medial femoral condyle,
replace the camera with a switching stick or trocar, and gently push through the
intercondylar notch to enter the posterior space.
Replace the switching stick or trocar with the camera to view the posterior compartment.
Switching to a 70° camera may aid in attaining better visualization.
This can also be done by visualizing with the camera in the anteromedial portal while
placing a blunt switching rod into the posteromedial compartment through the
anterolateral portal. Then the canula and camera can be moved back to the anterolateral
portal to visualize the posteromedial compartment.
A posteromedial portal can be established under direct visualization once in the posterior
portal.
Typically posterior to the medial collateral ligament, 1 cm proximal to joint line
A spinal needle can be used to triangulate at the entry point.
Transillumination of the skin may help avoid iatrogenic injury to the saphenous nerve.
A straight hemostat may be helpful to bluntly spread down to the posteromedial capsule
and puncture the capsule under direct visualization.
Posterolateral compartment
Direct visualization
Similar to the modified Gillquist procedure of the posteromedial compartment, the camera
is introduced from the anteromedial portal between the lateral border of the ACL and
medial border of the lateral femoral condyle.
Typically between the lateral collateral ligament and biceps tendon, 1 cm proximal to joint
line
Use a spinal needle to triangulate and create the portal.
Transseptal5
Place the knee in 90° to allow the popliteal vessels to move posteriorly.
Place the camera in the posteromedial portal and visualize the posterior compartment.
Leave sheath in place and remove camera.
Then, place camera in the posterolateral portal.

Under direct visualization, place a blunt obturator through the posteromedial sheath and
gently guide it into the posterolateral compartment, staying posterior to the PCL and anterior
to the posterior capsule.
Postoperative Management

Postoperative Management
Postoperative management may range from full–weight-bearing to the use of a brace
with weight-bearing restrictions. In determining postoperative restrictions, the surgeons
should consider whether any regional blocks were used. For most procedures, passive
range of motion should be initiated soon after surgery, with the structures surgically
managed driving postoperative rehabilitation protocols.
Complications

Complications
The overall complication rate after knee arthroscopy ranges from 1% to 5%. Procedure
complexity appears to correlate with complication rate, with PCL reconstruction, ACL
reconstruction, and meniscal repair being associated with complication rates of
approximately 20%, 9% and 7.6%, respectively.6 Chondroplasty and meniscectomy are
associated with complication rates less than 4%.6
Septic arthritis after knee arthroscopy is rare but may account for 5% of pyogenic
arthritis cases.7,8 Other rare surgical complications include postoperative hemarthrosis,
loss of motion, and a retained foreign body.9,10 Nerve injuries occur in less than 1% of
patients; however, they may be underreported.11,12 Iatrogenic nerve injury to the
saphenous (posteromedial portal) or common peroneal nerve (posterolateral portal)
must be considered during portal placement.10 The overall risk of deep vein thrombosis
after knee arthroscopy without prophylaxis is approximately 10%, whereas the risk of
proximal deep vein thrombosis is approximately 2%.13,14 The risk of symptomatic deep

vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism is less than 1%.15 Other medical complications
are rare (<1%), and anesthetic complications are similarly uncommon.6
Outcomes

Outcomes
Outcomes after knee arthroscopy vary widely, depending on the reason for arthroscopy.
For simple knee arthroscopy, patients can expect to return to activity in as few as 4 to 6
weeks postoperatively. Diagnostic arthroscopy also plays a key role in the staging of
complex meniscal and cartilage pathologies and in revision procedures. For patients with
degenerative conditions, knee arthroscopy may afford short-term benefits in pain
reduction but usually affords little long-term utility.16
